# API Reference

A complete reference to all the SQL scalar functions, aggregate functions,
table functions, and virtual tables inside `sqlite-tg`.

::: warning
`sqlite-tg` is pre-v1, so expect breaking changes.
:::

## Meta functions {#meta}

### `tg_version()` {#tg_version}

Returns the version string of `sqlite-tg`.

```sql
select tg_version();
-- 'v0.0.1-alpha.21'
```

### `tg_debug()` {#tg_debug}

Returns fuller debug information of `sqlite-tg`, including the build date and commit of `sqlite-tg` and the vendored [`tg`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg) library.

```sql
select tg_debug();
-- 'sqlite-tg version: v0....
-- sqlite-tg date: ...
-- sqlite-tg commit: ...'
```

## Constructors {#constructors}

### `tg_point(x, y)` {#tg_point}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
point geometry with the given `x` and `y` values. This value will appear
to be `NULL` on direct access, and is meant for performance critical SQL
queries where you want to avoid serializing/de-serializing.

`tg_point(x, y, z)` also accepts a third argument to construct a point
with a Z coordinate, and `tg_point(x, y, z, m)` a fourth to also add an M
coordinate. There is no way to construct an M-only point (with no Z) —
use [`tg_geom()`](#tg_geom) with `POINT M (...)` WKT text instead.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_point(1, 2));
-- 'POINT(1 2)'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_point(1, 2, 3));
-- 'POINT(1 2 3)'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_point(1, 2, 3, 4));
-- 'POINT(1 2 3 4)'
```

### `tg_line(p1, p2, ..., pN)` {#tg_line}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
LineString geometry made up of the given points, in order. Input
arguments must be Point geometries, in any
[supported format](/introduction#supported-formats).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_line(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(1, 1), tg_point(2, 0)));
-- 'LINESTRING(0 0,1 1,2 0)'
```

### `tg_linestring(p1, p2, ..., pN)` {#tg_linestring}

An alias of [`tg_line()`](#tg_line) — same implementation, provided for
familiarity with the WKT `LINESTRING` type name. Note that any error
messages it raises will still refer to `tg_line()`.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_linestring(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(1, 1)));
-- 'LINESTRING(0 0,1 1)'
```

### `tg_ring(p1, p2, ..., pN)` {#tg_ring}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a ring
made up of the given points, in order. Input arguments must be Point
geometries, in any [supported format](/introduction#supported-formats).
A ring can always be used anywhere a Polygon or generic geometry is
expected (see [`tg_poly_exterior()`](#tg_poly_exterior)), and is the
input type expected by [`tg_polygon()`](#tg_polygon).

A ring is always treated as geometrically closed — the segment from the
last point back to the first is implied even if you don't repeat it —
but `tg_to_wkt()`/`tg_to_geojson()` output echoes back exactly the
points you passed in. Repeat the first point as the last argument if you
want conventional closed-ring WKT/GeoJSON text.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_ring(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(10, 0), tg_point(10, 10)));
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10))'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_ring(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(10, 0), tg_point(10, 10), tg_point(0, 0)));
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10,0 0))'
```

### `tg_polygon(exterior, hole1, ..., holeN)` {#tg_polygon}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
Polygon geometry from the given exterior ring and, optionally, one or
more interior holes. Every argument must be a ring — either from
[`tg_ring()`](#tg_ring)/[`tg_poly_exterior()`](#tg_poly_exterior)/[`tg_holes_each()`](#tg_holes_each),
or a Polygon geometry with no holes of its own (its exterior ring is
used). A Polygon argument that itself has holes is rejected, since
silently using only its exterior would drop that data.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_polygon(
    tg_ring(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(10, 0), tg_point(10, 10), tg_point(0, 10), tg_point(0, 0))
  )
);
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10,0 10,0 0))'
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_polygon(
    tg_ring(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(10, 0), tg_point(10, 10), tg_point(0, 10), tg_point(0, 0)),
    tg_ring(tg_point(1, 1), tg_point(2, 1), tg_point(2, 2), tg_point(1, 2), tg_point(1, 1))
  )
);
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10,0 10,0 0),(1 1,2 1,2 2,1 2,1 1))'
```

### `tg_multipoint(p1, p2, ..., pN)` {#tg_multipoint}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
MultiPoint geometry with the given points. Input arguments must be Point
geometries, in any [supported format](/introduction#supported-formats).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_multipoint(tg_point(1, 1), tg_point(2, 2)));
-- 'MULTIPOINT(1 1,2 2)'
```

### `tg_multilinestring(l1, l2, ..., lN)` {#tg_multilinestring}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
MultiLineString geometry with the given LineStrings. Input arguments
must be LineString geometries, in any
[supported format](/introduction#supported-formats).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_multilinestring(
    tg_line(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(1, 1)),
    tg_line(tg_point(2, 2), tg_point(3, 3))
  )
);
-- 'MULTILINESTRING((0 0,1 1),(2 2,3 3))'
```

### `tg_multipolygon(p1, p2, ..., pN)` {#tg_multipolygon}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
MultiPolygon geometry with the given Polygons. Input arguments must be
Polygon geometries (including bare rings, which upcast to Polygon), in
any [supported format](/introduction#supported-formats).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_multipolygon(
    'POLYGON((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 0))',
    'POLYGON((10 10, 11 10, 11 11, 10 10))'
  )
);
-- 'MULTIPOLYGON(((0 0,1 0,1 1,0 0)),((10 10,11 10,11 11,10 10)))'
```

### `tg_geometrycollection(g1, g2, ..., gN)` {#tg_geometrycollection}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns a
GeometryCollection geometry with the given geometries, which may be of
mixed types (including nested GeometryCollections).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_geometrycollection('POINT(1 1)', 'LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)')
);
-- 'GEOMETRYCOLLECTION(POINT(1 1),LINESTRING(0 0,1 1))'
```

### `tg_geom(input, $index)` {#tg_geom}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that parses
`input` (in any [supported format](/introduction#supported-formats))
into a geometry, optionally building an internal index. The optional
second argument selects the
[tg index type](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/POLYGON_INDEXING.md)
and must be one of `'none'`, `'natural'`, or `'ystripes'`.

Unrecognized index options raise an error.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_geom('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}'));
-- 'POINT(0 1)'
select tg_type(tg_geom('POLYGON((30 10, 40 40, 20 40, 10 20, 30 10))', 'ystripes'));
-- 'Polygon'
select tg_geom('POINT(0 1)', 'not-an-index');
-- error: unrecognized index option. Should be one of none/natural/ystripes
```

### `tg_poly_exterior(polygon)` {#tg_poly_exterior}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns the
exterior ring of the given Polygon geometry, dropping any holes.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_poly_exterior('POLYGON((30 10, 40 40, 20 40, 10 20, 30 10), (20 30, 35 35, 30 20, 20 30))')
);
-- 'POLYGON((30 10,40 40,20 40,10 20,30 10))'
```

### `tg_rect(minX, minY, maxX, maxY) / tg_rect(minP, maxP)` {#tg_rect}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns the
equivalent closed-ring Polygon geometry for the given rectangle:
`POLYGON((minx miny, maxx miny, maxx maxy, minx maxy, minx miny))`, with
counter-clockwise winding and the closing point repeated. `tg` has no
`tg_geom` representation of a rect (see `struct tg_rect`), so this is
how it composes with every other `sqlite-tg` function. The two-argument
form takes Point geometries, in any
[supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), for the min/max
corners.

No normalization is applied: if `minX > maxX` (or `minY > maxY`), the
polygon is built exactly as given. Since the result is an ordinary
Polygon geometry, it composes with predicates like any other geometry.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_rect(0, 0, 1, 1));
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,1 0,1 1,0 1,0 0))'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_rect(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(1, 1)));
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,1 0,1 1,0 1,0 0))'
select tg_intersects(tg_rect(0, 0, 10, 10), tg_point(5, 5));
-- 1
```

### `tg_segment(aX, aY, bX, bY) / tg_segment(aP, bP)` {#tg_segment}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) that returns the
equivalent 2-point LineString geometry for the given segment:
`LINESTRING(ax ay, bx by)`. `tg` has no `tg_geom` representation of a
segment (see `struct tg_segment`), so this is how it composes with every
other `sqlite-tg` function. The two-argument form takes Point
geometries, in any [supported format](/introduction#supported-formats),
for the two endpoints.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(tg_segment(0, 0, 1, 1));
-- 'LINESTRING(0 0,1 1)'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_segment(tg_point(0, 0), tg_point(1, 1)));
-- 'LINESTRING(0 0,1 1)'
```

## Aggregate constructors {#aggregates}

These are [aggregate functions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_aggfunc.html)
that build a single geometry from a group of rows. Note that the order of
aggregated rows is only guaranteed when the query has an explicit
`order by`.

### `tg_group_multipoint(point)` {#tg_group_multipoint}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a MultiPoint geometry from the aggregated Point
geometries.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_multipoint(tg_point(value ->> 0, value ->> 1))
)
from json_each('[[1, 1], [2, 2], [3, 3]]');
-- 'MULTIPOINT(1 1,2 2,3 3)'
```

### `tg_group_line(point)` {#tg_group_line}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a LineString geometry from the aggregated Point
geometries, in row order. A zero-row aggregate produces
`LINESTRING EMPTY`, matching
[`tg_group_multipoint()`](#tg_group_multipoint).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_line(tg_point(value ->> 0, value ->> 1))
)
from json_each('[[1, 1], [2, 2]]');
-- 'LINESTRING(1 1,2 2)'
```

### `tg_group_ring(point)` {#tg_group_ring}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a ring from the aggregated Point geometries, in row
order — same closing-point behavior as [`tg_ring()`](#tg_ring). A
zero-row aggregate produces the same empty-ring shape as `tg_ring()`
with no arguments.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_ring(tg_point(value ->> 0, value ->> 1))
)
from json_each('[[0, 0], [10, 0], [10, 10]]');
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10))'
```

### `tg_group_polygon(ring)` {#tg_group_polygon}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a Polygon geometry from the aggregated rings: the
first row is the exterior and any subsequent rows are holes. Each row
follows the same ring convention as [`tg_polygon()`](#tg_polygon) — a
bare ring upcast, or a hole-free Polygon geometry — and a
Polygon-with-holes row is rejected for the same reason. A zero-row
aggregate produces `POLYGON EMPTY`, matching `tg_polygon()` with no
arguments. Use [`tg_group_ring()`](#tg_group_ring) to build rings first
if you need holes assembled separately.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_polygon(value)
)
from json_each('[
  "POLYGON((0 0, 10 0, 10 10, 0 10, 0 0))",
  "POLYGON((1 1, 2 1, 2 2, 1 2, 1 1))"
]');
-- 'POLYGON((0 0,10 0,10 10,0 10,0 0),(1 1,2 1,2 2,1 2,1 1))'
```

### `tg_group_multilinestring(line)` {#tg_group_multilinestring}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a MultiLineString geometry from the aggregated
LineString geometries.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_multilinestring(value)
)
from json_each('["LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)", "LINESTRING(2 2, 3 3)"]');
-- 'MULTILINESTRING((0 0,1 1),(2 2,3 3))'
```

### `tg_group_multipolygon(polygon)` {#tg_group_multipolygon}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a MultiPolygon geometry from the aggregated Polygon
geometries.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_multipolygon(value)
)
from json_each('["POLYGON((0 0, 1 0, 1 1, 0 0))", "POLYGON((2 2, 3 2, 3 3, 2 2))"]');
-- 'MULTIPOLYGON(((0 0,1 0,1 1,0 0)),((2 2,3 2,3 3,2 2)))'
```

### `tg_group_geometrycollection(geometry)` {#tg_group_geometrycollection}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that builds a GeometryCollection from the aggregated
geometries, which may be of mixed types. Named to match the
underscore-free `tg_multipoint`/`tg_multilinestring`/`tg_multipolygon`/
`tg_geometrycollection` convention.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_geometrycollection(value)
)
from json_each('["POINT(1 1)", "LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)"]');
-- 'GEOMETRYCOLLECTION(POINT(1 1),LINESTRING(0 0,1 1))'
```

### `tg_group_geometry_collection(geometry)` {#tg_group_geometry_collection}

A **deprecated** alias of
[`tg_group_geometrycollection()`](#tg_group_geometrycollection) — same
implementation, same behavior, kept registered for backwards
compatibility. Prefer `tg_group_geometrycollection()` in new code.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_geometry_collection(value)
)
from json_each('["POINT(1 1)", "LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)"]');
-- 'GEOMETRYCOLLECTION(POINT(1 1),LINESTRING(0 0,1 1))'
```

### `tg_group_bbox(geometry)` {#tg_group_bbox}

A [pointer function](/introduction#pointer-functions) and aggregate
function that returns the bounding box of all aggregated geometries, as
a Polygon geometry.

```sql
select tg_to_wkt(
  tg_group_bbox(value)
)
from json_each('["POINT(1 1)", "POINT(5 9)"]');
-- 'POLYGON((1 1,5 1,5 9,1 9,1 1))'
```

### `tg_group_feature_collection_geojson(geometry, $properties)` {#tg_group_feature_collection_geojson}

An aggregate function that builds a GeoJSON `FeatureCollection` string
from the aggregated geometries. The optional second argument provides
the `properties` object for each feature.

```sql
select tg_group_feature_collection_geojson(value)
from json_each('["POINT(1 1)", "POINT(2 2)"]');
-- '{"type":"FeatureCollection", "features": [{"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type":"Point","coordinates":[1,1]}, "properties": {}},{"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type":"Point","coordinates":[2,2]}, "properties": {}}]}'

select tg_group_feature_collection_geojson(
  value,
  json_object('idx', key)
)
from json_each('["POINT(1 1)", "POINT(2 2)"]');
-- '{"type":"FeatureCollection", "features": [{"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type":"Point","coordinates":[1,1]}, "properties": {"idx":0}},{"type": "Feature", "geometry": {"type":"Point","coordinates":[2,2]}, "properties": {"idx":1}}]}'
```

## Conversions {#convertors}

### `tg_to_geojson(geometry)` {#tg_to_geojson}

Converts the given geometry into a GeoJSON string. Inputs can be in
[any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), including WKT,
WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_geojson()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_geojson).

```sql
select tg_to_geojson('POINT(0 1)');
-- '{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}'
select tg_to_geojson(X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000f03f');
-- '{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}'
select tg_to_geojson('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- '{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}'
select tg_to_geojson(tg_point(0, 1));
-- '{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}'
```

### `tg_to_wkb(geometry)` {#tg_to_wkb}

Converts the given geometry into a WKB blob. Inputs can be in
[any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), including WKT,
WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_wkb()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_wkb).

```sql
select tg_to_wkb('POINT(0 1)');
-- X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000F03F'
select tg_to_wkb(X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000f03f');
-- X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000F03F'
select tg_to_wkb('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000F03F'
select tg_to_wkb(tg_point(0, 1));
-- X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000F03F'
```

### `tg_to_wkt(geometry)` {#tg_to_wkt}

Converts the given geometry into a WKT string. Inputs can be in
[any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), including WKT,
WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_wkt()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_wkt).

```sql
select tg_to_wkt('POINT(0 1)');
-- 'POINT(0 1)'
select tg_to_wkt(X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000f03f');
-- 'POINT(0 1)'
select tg_to_wkt('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- 'POINT(0 1)'
select tg_to_wkt(tg_point(0, 1));
-- 'POINT(0 1)'
```

## Misc. {#misc}

### `tg_type(geometry)` {#tg_type}

Returns a string describing the type of the provided `geometry`. Inputs
can be in [any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats),
including WKT, WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_type_string()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_type_string).

Possible values:

- `"Point"`
- `"LineString"`
- `"Polygon"`
- `"MultiPoint"`
- `"MultiLineString"`
- `"MultiPolygon"`
- `"GeometryCollection"`
- `"Unknown"`

```sql
select tg_type('POINT (30 10)');
-- 'Point'
select tg_type('LINESTRING (30 10, 10 30, 40 40)');
-- 'LineString'
select tg_type('POLYGON ((30 10, 40 40, 20 40, 10 20, 30 10))');
-- 'Polygon'
select tg_type('MULTIPOINT (10 40, 40 30, 20 20, 30 10)');
-- 'MultiPoint'
select tg_type('MULTIPOLYGON (((30 20, 45 40, 10 40, 30 20)),((15 5, 40 10, 10 20, 5 10, 15 5)))');
-- 'MultiPolygon'
select tg_type('GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (POINT (40 10),LINESTRING (10 10, 20 20, 10 40))');
-- 'GeometryCollection'
```

### `tg_extra_json(geometry)` {#tg_extra_json}

If the original geometry is a GeoJSON with extra fields such as `id` or
`property`, those extra fields will be returned in a JSON object.
Returns `NULL` if there are no extra fields.

```sql
select tg_extra_json('{
  "type": "Point",
  "coordinates": [-118.2097812,34.0437074]
}');
-- NULL
select tg_extra_json('{
  "id": "ASG0017",
  "type": "Point",
  "coordinates": [-118.2097812,34.0437074],
  "properties": {"color": "red"}
}');
-- '{"id":"ASG0017","properties":{"color": "red"}}'
```

### `tg_dims(geometry)` {#tg_dims}

Returns the number of coordinate dimensions of the given `geometry`: `2`
for plain X/Y geometries, `3` when it carries a Z or M coordinate, and
`4` when it carries both. Inputs can be in
[any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), including WKT,
WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_dims()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_dims).

```sql
select tg_dims('POINT(0 1)');
-- 2
```

### `tg_is_empty(geometry)` {#tg_is_empty}

Returns `1` if the given `geometry` is an empty geometry (such as
`POINT EMPTY`), `0` otherwise. Inputs can be in
[any supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), including WKT,
WKB, and GeoJSON. Based on
[`tg_geom_is_empty()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_is_empty).

```sql
select tg_is_empty('POINT EMPTY');
-- 1
select tg_is_empty('POINT(0 1)');
-- 0
```

### `tg_is_feature(geometry)` {#tg_is_feature}

Returns `1` if the given `geometry` was parsed from a GeoJSON `Feature`,
`0` otherwise. Based on
[`tg_geom_is_feature()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_is_feature).

```sql
select tg_is_feature('{"type":"Feature","geometry":{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]},"properties":{}}');
-- 1
select tg_is_feature('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- 0
```

### `tg_is_featurecollection(geometry)` {#tg_is_featurecollection}

Returns `1` if the given `geometry` was parsed from a GeoJSON
`FeatureCollection`, `0` otherwise. Based on
[`tg_geom_is_featurecollection()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_is_featurecollection).

```sql
select tg_is_featurecollection('{"type":"FeatureCollection","features":[]}');
-- 1
select tg_is_featurecollection('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- 0
```

### `tg_memsize(geometry)` {#tg_memsize}

Returns the number of bytes of memory used to store the given `geometry`
in its parsed, in-memory representation. Useful for estimating the cost
of indexed blobs, such as those created with `tg_geom(x, 'ystripes')`.
Based on
[`tg_geom_memsize()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_memsize).

```sql
select tg_memsize('POINT(0 1)');
-- 24
```

## Validation {#validate}

### `tg_valid_geojson(text)` {#tg_valid_geojson}

Returns `1` if the given text is valid GeoJSON, `0` otherwise.

```sql
select tg_valid_geojson('{"type":"Point","coordinates":[0,1]}');
-- 1
select tg_valid_geojson('{"type": "not-geojson"}');
-- 0
```

### `tg_valid_wkt(text)` {#tg_valid_wkt}

Returns `1` if the given text is valid WKT, `0` otherwise.

```sql
select tg_valid_wkt('POINT(0 1)');
-- 1
select tg_valid_wkt('POINT()');
-- 0
```

### `tg_valid_wkb(blob)` {#tg_valid_wkb}

Returns `1` if the given blob is valid WKB, `0` otherwise.

```sql
select tg_valid_wkb(X'01010000000000000000000000000000000000f03f');
-- 1
select tg_valid_wkb(X'00');
-- 0
```

## Coordinates and bounding boxes {#coords}

Coordinate and bounding box accessors.

### `tg_x(point)` {#tg_x}

Returns the X coordinate of the given Point geometry. Raises an error if
the input is not a Point.

```sql
select tg_x('POINT(1 2)');
-- 1.0
select tg_x('LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)');
-- error: tg_x() expected a Point geometry, found LineString
```

### `tg_y(point)` {#tg_y}

Returns the Y coordinate of the given Point geometry. Raises an error if
the input is not a Point.

```sql
select tg_y('POINT(1 2)');
-- 2.0
select tg_y('LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)');
-- error: tg_y() expected a Point geometry, found LineString
```

### `tg_has_z(geometry)` {#tg_has_z}

Returns `1` if the given geometry has a Z coordinate, `0` otherwise.
Works on any geometry type, not just Points.

```sql
select tg_has_z('POINT(1 2)');
-- 0
select tg_has_z('POINT Z (1 2 3)');
-- 1
select tg_has_z('LINESTRING Z (0 0 1, 1 1 1)');
-- 1
```

### `tg_has_m(geometry)` {#tg_has_m}

Returns `1` if the given geometry has an M coordinate, `0` otherwise.
Works on any geometry type, not just Points.

```sql
select tg_has_m('POINT(1 2)');
-- 0
select tg_has_m('POINT ZM (1 2 3 4)');
-- 1
```

### `tg_z(point)` {#tg_z}

Returns the Z coordinate of the given Point geometry, or `NULL` if it
has no Z coordinate. Raises an error if the input is not a Point. `NULL`
is used instead of `0` for a missing Z so it's distinguishable from an
actual Z value of `0` — check with [`tg_has_z()`](#tg_has_z) if you need
to tell "no Z" apart from "Z is 0".

```sql
select tg_z('POINT(1 2)');
-- NULL
select tg_z('POINT Z (1 2 3)');
-- 3.0
select tg_z('LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)');
-- error: tg_z() expected a Point geometry, found LineString
```

### `tg_m(point)` {#tg_m}

Returns the M coordinate of the given Point geometry, or `NULL` if it
has no M coordinate. Raises an error if the input is not a Point. Same
`NULL`-for-missing convention as [`tg_z()`](#tg_z).

```sql
select tg_m('POINT(1 2)');
-- NULL
select tg_m('POINT ZM (1 2 3 4)');
-- 4.0
select tg_m('LINESTRING(0 0, 1 1)');
-- error: tg_m() expected a Point geometry, found LineString
```

### `tg_min_x(geometry)` {#tg_min_x}

Returns the minimum X coordinate of the given geometry's bounding box.
Based on
[`tg_geom_rect()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_rect).
Useful for populating an [R-Tree](https://www.sqlite.org/rtree.html)
index alongside a geometry column, though the
[`tg_bbox`](#tg_bbox) table function and the [`tg0`](#tg0) virtual table
can do this for you.

```sql
select tg_min_x('POLYGON((1 1, 2 2, 3 3, 1 1))');
-- 1.0
```

### `tg_min_y(geometry)` {#tg_min_y}

Returns the minimum Y coordinate of the given geometry's bounding box.
Based on
[`tg_geom_rect()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_rect).

```sql
select tg_min_y('POLYGON((1 1, 2 2, 3 3, 1 1))');
-- 1.0
```

### `tg_max_x(geometry)` {#tg_max_x}

Returns the maximum X coordinate of the given geometry's bounding box.
Based on
[`tg_geom_rect()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_rect).

```sql
select tg_max_x('POLYGON((1 1, 2 2, 3 3, 1 1))');
-- 3.0
```

### `tg_max_y(geometry)` {#tg_max_y}

Returns the maximum Y coordinate of the given geometry's bounding box.
Based on
[`tg_geom_rect()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_rect).

```sql
select tg_max_y('POLYGON((1 1, 2 2, 3 3, 1 1))');
-- 3.0
```

## Predicates {#predicates}

Every predicate accepts two geometries `a` and `b`, in any
[supported format](/introduction#supported-formats), and returns `1` or
`0`. All raise an error if either input is not a valid geometry.

### `tg_intersects(a, b)` {#tg_intersects}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry intersects the `b` geometry, otherwise
returns `0`. Based on
[`tg_geom_intersects()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_intersects).

```sql
select tg_intersects(
  'LINESTRING (0 0, 2 2)',
  'LINESTRING (1 0, 1 2)'
);
-- 1
select tg_intersects(
  'POLYGON((
    -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113,
    -122.51610563264538 37.69618409220847,
    -122.35290547288255 37.69618409220847,
    -122.35290547288255 37.81424532146113,
    -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113
  ))',
  'POINT(-122.4075 37.787994)'
);
-- 1
select tg_intersects(
  'POLYGON((
    -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113,
    -122.51610563264538 37.69618409220847,
    -122.35290547288255 37.69618409220847,
    -122.35290547288255 37.81424532146113,
    -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113
  ))',
  'POINT(-73.985130 40.758896)'
);
-- 0
```

### `tg_disjoint(a, b)` {#tg_disjoint}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry shares no point with the `b` geometry,
otherwise returns `0`. The inverse of [`tg_intersects`](#tg_intersects).
Based on
[`tg_geom_disjoint()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_disjoint).

```sql
select tg_disjoint('POINT(5 5)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 1
select tg_disjoint('POINT(1 1)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 0
```

### `tg_contains(a, b)` {#tg_contains}

Returns `1` if the `b` geometry is fully contained inside the `a`
geometry, otherwise returns `0`. Like [`tg_within`](#tg_within) with the
arguments swapped, but with slightly stricter "boundary" rules — a
geometry lying only on the boundary of `a` is not "contained". If you
want to test full coverage, see [`tg_covers()`](#tg_covers). Based on
[`tg_geom_contains()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_contains).

```sql
select tg_contains('POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))', 'POINT(1 1)');
-- 1
select tg_contains('POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))', 'POINT(0 1)');
-- 0
```

### `tg_within(a, b)` {#tg_within}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry is fully contained inside the `b`
geometry, otherwise returns `0`. Like [`tg_contains`](#tg_contains) with
the arguments swapped. If you want to test full coverage, see
[`tg_coveredby()`](#tg_coveredby). Based on
[`tg_geom_within()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_within).

```sql
select tg_within('POINT(1 1)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 1
select tg_within('POINT(5 5)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 0
```

### `tg_covers(a, b)` {#tg_covers}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry covers every point of the `b` geometry
(boundary points included), otherwise returns `0`. Based on
[`tg_geom_covers()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_covers).

```sql
select tg_covers('POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))', 'POINT(0 1)');
-- 1
select tg_covers('POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))', 'POINT(5 5)');
-- 0
```

### `tg_coveredby(a, b)` {#tg_coveredby}

Returns `1` if every point of the `a` geometry (boundary points
included) is covered by the `b` geometry, otherwise returns `0`. Like
[`tg_covers`](#tg_covers) with the arguments swapped. Based on
[`tg_geom_coveredby()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_coveredby).

```sql
select tg_coveredby('POINT(0 1)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 1
select tg_coveredby('POINT(5 5)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 0
```

### `tg_touches(a, b)` {#tg_touches}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry touches the `b` geometry — they share at
least one point, but their interiors do not intersect. Otherwise returns
`0`. Based on
[`tg_geom_touches()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_touches).

```sql
select tg_touches('POINT(0 1)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 1
select tg_touches('POINT(1 1)', 'POLYGON((0 0, 2 0, 2 2, 0 2, 0 0))');
-- 0
```

### `tg_equals(a, b)` {#tg_equals}

Returns `1` if the `a` geometry is spatially equal to the `b` geometry,
otherwise returns `0`. Based on
[`tg_geom_equals()`](https://github.com/tidwall/tg/blob/main/docs/API.md#tg_geom_equals).

```sql
select tg_equals('POINT(1 1)', 'POINT(1 1)');
-- 1
select tg_equals('POINT(1 1)', 'POINT(2 2)');
-- 0
```

## Table functions {#table-functions}

Each of these table functions iterates over the components of a single
geometry. The geometry-valued columns are
[pointer values](/introduction#pointer-functions), so serialize them with
`tg_to_wkt()` and friends to read them. `rowid` is the zero-based index
of the component.

### `tg_points_each(geometry)` {#tg_points_each}

Iterates over every Point in the given MultiPoint geometry, in the `point` column.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(point) as point
from tg_points_each('MULTIPOINT (10 40, 40 30, 20 20)');
/*
┌───────┬────────────────┐
│ rowid │ point          │
├───────┼────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POINT(10 40)' │
│ 1     │ 'POINT(40 30)' │
│ 2     │ 'POINT(20 20)' │
└───────┴────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_lines_each(geometry)` {#tg_lines_each}

Iterates over every LineString in the given MultiLineString geometry, in the `line` column.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(line) as line
from tg_lines_each('MULTILINESTRING ((10 10, 20 20), (40 40, 30 30))');
/*
┌───────┬───────────────────────────┐
│ rowid │ line                      │
├───────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'LINESTRING(10 10,20 20)' │
│ 1     │ 'LINESTRING(40 40,30 30)' │
└───────┴───────────────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_line_points_each(line)` {#tg_line_points_each}

Iterates over every Point of the given LineString geometry, in the `point` column. Errors on non-LineString input.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(point) as point
from tg_line_points_each('LINESTRING (10 10, 20 20, 10 40)');
/*
┌───────┬────────────────┐
│ rowid │ point          │
├───────┼────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POINT(10 10)' │
│ 1     │ 'POINT(20 20)' │
│ 2     │ 'POINT(10 40)' │
└───────┴────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_line_segments_each(line)` {#tg_line_segments_each}

Iterates over every segment of the given LineString geometry, as flat `ax`, `ay`, `bx`, `by` columns. Errors on non-LineString input.

```sql
select rowid, ax, ay, bx, by
from tg_line_segments_each('LINESTRING (10 10, 20 20, 10 40)');
/*
┌───────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
│ rowid │ ax   │ ay   │ bx   │ by   │
├───────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
│ 0     │ 10.0 │ 10.0 │ 20.0 │ 20.0 │
│ 1     │ 20.0 │ 20.0 │ 10.0 │ 40.0 │
└───────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
*/
```

### `tg_polygons_each(geometry)` {#tg_polygons_each}

Iterates over every Polygon in the given MultiPolygon geometry, in the `polygon` column.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(polygon) as polygon
from tg_polygons_each('MULTIPOLYGON (((30 20, 45 40, 10 40, 30 20)),((15 5, 40 10, 10 20, 15 5)))');
/*
┌───────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ rowid │ polygon                              │
├───────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POLYGON((30 20,45 40,10 40,30 20))' │
│ 1     │ 'POLYGON((15 5,40 10,10 20,15 5))'   │
└───────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_holes_each(polygon)` {#tg_holes_each}

Iterates over every hole (interior ring) of the given Polygon geometry, in the `hole` column.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(hole) as hole
from tg_holes_each('POLYGON(
  (0 0, 10 0, 10 10, 0 10, 0 0),
  (1 1, 2 1, 2 2, 1 2, 1 1),
  (5 5, 6 5, 6 6, 5 6, 5 5)
)');
/*
┌───────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
│ rowid │ hole                             │
├───────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POLYGON((1 1,2 1,2 2,1 2,1 1))' │
│ 1     │ 'POLYGON((5 5,6 5,6 6,5 6,5 5))' │
└───────┴──────────────────────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_ring_points_each(ring)` {#tg_ring_points_each}

Iterates over every Point of the given ring, in the `point` column. The ring argument accepts either the upcast ring pointers produced by [`tg_poly_exterior()`](#tg_poly_exterior)/[`tg_holes_each()`](#tg_holes_each), or a plain Polygon geometry, in which case its exterior ring is used. Errors on any other geometry type.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(point) as point
from tg_ring_points_each(tg_poly_exterior('POLYGON ((0 0, 10 0, 10 10, 0 10, 0 0))'));
/*
┌───────┬────────────────┐
│ rowid │ point          │
├───────┼────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POINT(0 0)'   │
│ 1     │ 'POINT(10 0)'  │
│ 2     │ 'POINT(10 10)' │
│ 3     │ 'POINT(0 10)'  │
│ 4     │ 'POINT(0 0)'   │
└───────┴────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_ring_segments_each(ring)` {#tg_ring_segments_each}

Iterates over every segment of the given ring, as flat `ax`, `ay`, `bx`, `by` columns. Accepts the same ring/Polygon input as [`tg_ring_points_each()`](#tg_ring_points_each).

```sql
select rowid, ax, ay, bx, by
from tg_ring_segments_each(tg_poly_exterior('POLYGON ((0 0, 10 0, 10 10, 0 10, 0 0))'));
/*
┌───────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
│ rowid │ ax   │ ay   │ bx   │ by   │
├───────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
│ 0     │ 0.0  │ 0.0  │ 10.0 │ 0.0  │
│ 1     │ 10.0 │ 0.0  │ 10.0 │ 10.0 │
│ 2     │ 10.0 │ 10.0 │ 0.0  │ 10.0 │
│ 3     │ 0.0  │ 10.0 │ 0.0  │ 0.0  │
└───────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
*/
```

### `tg_geometries_each(geometry)` {#tg_geometries_each}

Iterates over every geometry in the given GeometryCollection, in the `geometry` column.

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(geometry) as geometry
from tg_geometries_each('GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (POINT (40 10), LINESTRING (10 10, 20 20, 10 40))');
/*
┌───────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ rowid │ geometry                        │
├───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POINT(40 10)'                  │
│ 1     │ 'LINESTRING(10 10,20 20,10 40)' │
└───────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_each(geometry)` {#tg_each}

An alias of [`tg_geometries_each`](#tg_geometries_each).

```sql
select rowid, tg_to_wkt(geometry) as geometry
from tg_each('GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (POINT (40 10), LINESTRING (10 10, 20 20, 10 40))');
/*
┌───────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ rowid │ geometry                        │
├───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
│ 0     │ 'POINT(40 10)'                  │
│ 1     │ 'LINESTRING(10 10,20 20,10 40)' │
└───────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
*/
```

### `tg_bbox(geometry)` {#tg_bbox}

Returns a single row with the bounding box of the given geometry, in the `minX`, `maxX`, `minY`, and `maxY` columns. Useful for manually inserting geometries into an [R-Tree index](https://www.sqlite.org/rtree.html), though the [`tg0`](#tg0) virtual table does this for you automatically.

```sql
select * from tg_bbox('LINESTRING (30 10, 10 30, 40 40)');
/*
┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
│ minX │ maxX │ minY │ maxY │
├──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
│ 10.0 │ 40.0 │ 10.0 │ 40.0 │
└──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
*/
```

## Virtual tables {#virtual-tables}

### `tg0(aux1, aux2, ...)` {#tg0}

An experimental virtual table that stores geometries in the `_shape`
column, backed by an [R-Tree index](https://www.sqlite.org/rtree.html)
on their bounding boxes for accelerated spatial queries. Requires the
R-Tree extension to be compiled into the host SQLite. Any arguments
become auxiliary columns on the table. Expect breaking changes.

```sql
create virtual table businesses using tg0(name);
insert into businesses(rowid, _shape, name) values
  (1, tg_geom('POINT(-122.4075 37.787994)'), 'in sf'),
  (2, tg_geom('POINT(-73.985130 40.758896)'), 'in nyc');
select rowid, name
from businesses
where tg_intersects(_shape, 'POLYGON((
  -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113,
  -122.51610563264538 37.69618409220847,
  -122.35290547288255 37.69618409220847,
  -122.35290547288255 37.81424532146113,
  -122.51610563264538 37.81424532146113
))');
/*
┌───────┬─────────┐
│ rowid │ name    │
├───────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ 'in sf' │
└───────┴─────────┘
*/
```
